docs.text: Admin login For: whoever runs a server's admin endpoints, and developers of a client. You'll find: why an admin key alone isn't enough, the challenge, the token, the lockout, the settings, computing an answer, and what it doesn't protect against. An application's admin permissions (destroying data, changing the cluster) need a login as well as an admin role. The login proves the caller holds an admin key without the key crossing the network, and gives a short-lived token. The challenge client server │ GET /admin/challenge │ │◄──────────────── {"nonce": "9f2c41...", "expires_in": 60} │ │ │ client = sha256(key) │ │ hash = sha256(client) (the key's entry's) │ │ response = client XOR HMAC-SHA256(hash, nonce), hex│ │ POST /admin/login {"nonce", "response"} │ │◄──────────────── {"token": "q8Zr...", "expires_in": 900} │ │ │ an admin call │ │ Authorization: Bearer q8Zr... │ A key alone doesn't reach an admin endpoint. An admin's key works like a write key on the others; the admin endpoints need the token. The answer is SCRAM's (RFC 5802). The server computes the HMAC from the hash it holds, recovers client , and checks that its SHA-256 is the hash. So answering takes sha256(key) , which the entry doesn't give away: a stolen API_KEYS can't log in. A nonce is used once: it is gone after one answer, right or wrong, and after ADMIN_CHALLENGE_SECONDS . A captured answer can't be replayed. The token It names the key that logged in and when it expires ( ADMIN_TOKEN_SECONDS ), signed with SESSION_SECRET (HMAC-SHA256). The server keeps nothing of it, so it holds across a restart, and at every server with the same secret. It works only while its key does: removing or replacing the key in API_KEYS or API_KEYS_FILE , or giving it a role not built on admin, ends its logins at once (401: log in again). POST /admin/logout ends it early, at this server. Each admin call still needs its permission: a role operator=admin-manage may log in, but not call what needs manage ( Roles and permissions ). The lockout Wrong answers are counted per caller's address. After ADMIN_MAX_FAILURES in a row, that address gets 429 (with Retry-After ) for ADMIN_LOCKOUT_SECONDS , even for a right answer. Other addresses are not affected. Behind a reverse proxy, the address is the one it passes on: set UVICORN_FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS to the proxy's addresses, or every client shares the proxy's. Settings Setting Default What it does ADMIN_TOKEN_SECONDS 900 How long a login lasts ADMIN_CHALLENGE_SECONDS 60 How long a challenge's nonce can be answered ADMIN_MAX_FAILURES 5 Wrong answers in a row from one address before it is locked out... ADMIN_LOCKOUT_SECONDS 300 ...for this long SESSION_SECRET made at startup Signs the tokens: the same on every server, so a login works at all of them With keys, but none with an admin role, the admin endpoints are off (403). With an identity provider, a token with the admin role reaches them with no challenge ( OAuth and OIDC ). Computing an answer graph_security.admin_auth.answer(key, nonce) returns it. In any language: with client and hash the hex strings above, bytes(a ^ b for a, b in zip(bytes.fromhex(client), hmac.new(hash.encode(), nonce.encode(), "sha256").digest())).hex() Each application has a tool that logs in for you, reading the key from the environment, never the command line (sitelabs-graph-database: scripts/admin-token.py ; sitelabs-partitioned-graph: python -m app.tools admin ). Refusals Answer When 401 No token, a malformed, unknown or expired one; a wrong answer, or a nonce unknown, used or expired; a token whose key is gone 403 The admin endpoints are off: no key has an admin role 429 , with Retry-After Too many wrong answers from this address; or 10,000 challenges outstanding Every login, right or refused, and every logout goes to the application's audit hook. Neither a key nor a token is ever logged. What it doesn't protect against Keys, not users: no password policy or second factor. An identity provider gives both. No transport security of its own: tokens travel as bearer headers. Use TLS. A logout is per server: another server with the same secret takes the token until it expires, at most ADMIN_TOKEN_SECONDS .

docs.text: Development For: developers of this package. You'll find: the tests, changing it beside an application, releasing, and the documentation site. The tests pip install -e ".[test]" python -m pytest The tests make their own keys, tokens and certificates: no identity provider and no network. Changing it beside an application Install a checkout in place of the release an application pins, run the application's tests, then release: pip install --no-deps -e ../sitelabs-graph-security # in the application's environment The settings' names and defaults are shared: a new setting goes in SecuritySettings , in each application's Settings , and on the Settings page. Releasing Change the version in pyproject.toml ( 0.3.0 ), and move the changelog's Unreleased entries under the new release ( CHANGELOG.md ). Commit, tag ( v0.3.0 ) and push both. The tag publishes the release's documentation site. In each application, pin the new tag (its requirements.txt and lock file), and change its links to this site to the new release ( /sitelabs-graph-security/0.3/ ). The documentation site docs/ is published at https://sitelabs-com.github.io/sitelabs-graph-security/, one site per release, with mike : /0.2/ , /0.3/ ...: each release's site, for the code an application pins. Applications link to these. /latest/ : the newest. The site's root sends browsers there. .github/workflows/mkdocs.yml publishes the release in pyproject.toml on every push to main that changes the docs, and on every tag. The menu at the top of each page and the sidebar come from GROUPS in tools/docs.py : python tools/docs.py # write the menus and mkdocs.yml's nav python tools/docs.py --check # change nothing; fail if a file is out of date pip install -r requirements-docs.txt mkdocs serve # the site at http://127.0.0.1:8000, as you edit mkdocs build --strict # what the workflow builds, failing on a broken link

docs.text: In a FastAPI app For: developers of an application that runs this package. You'll find: registering the permissions, the parts the checks need, the checks on each call, the sign-in endpoints, the hooks, and the refusals. 1. The permissions Register the application's catalogue once, when its roles module is imported. Functions called without roles use it, and say so if there is none. from graph_security.roles import Catalogue, use CATALOGUE = use(Catalogue( {"query": "read queries", "write": "write queries", "load": "bulk loads", "manage": "the platform"}, read={"query"}, write={"write", "load"}, admin_only={"manage"})) BUILT_IN, parse_roles = CATALOGUE.built_in, CATALOGUE.parse_roles query is the permission a browser session keeps ( Browser sessions ): name the read permission so, or sessions do nothing. 2. The parts Security reads the application's security parts from each request, through parts(request) : an object with keys ( graph_security.keys.ApiKeys ), admin ( admin_auth.AdminAuth ), sessions ( sessions.Sessions ), limits ( limits.Limits , or None ) and oidc ( oidc.Oidc , or None ). The application makes them at startup from its settings, usually on app.state . 3. The checks on each call from fastapi import Depends, Request from graph_security.web import Security SECURITY = Security(parts=lambda request: request.app.state, settings=lambda request: get_settings(), cookie="app_session", sso_cookie="app_sso", on_caller=lambda request, p: ..., audit=...) @app.post("/query", dependencies=[Depends(SECURITY.permission("query")), Depends(SECURITY.running)]) def query(request: Request, ...): SECURITY.demand(request, "write") # once it knows the query writes What it does SECURITY.permission(name) A dependency: the caller (a key, a token, a session, or anyone when open), whose role has the permission. An admin permission needs an admin login or token too. Counts the call against the caller's rate SECURITY.demand(request, name) The same check, in the middle of a call: for a permission only the request's content shows SECURITY.running A dependency: one of the caller's MAX_RUNNING_PER_CALLER places, while the call runs SECURITY.caller(request) The caller already identified, or None SECURITY.is_open(request) No keys and no identity provider: every endpoint open 4. The sign-in endpoints app.include_router(SECURITY.session_router()) GET , POST and DELETE /session , and /console/sso/start and /console/sso/callback for signing in at the identity provider ( Browser sessions ). The admin login's endpoints ( /admin/challenge , /admin/login , /admin/logout ) stay in the application, calling AdminAuth ( Admin login ). 5. The hooks Hook Called on_caller(request, principal) As soon as the caller is known: for the logs and the application's request state on_admin(request) When a call needs an admin permission: for the audit log audit(action, message, level, **fields) For the sign-in lines ( session.start , session.end ) cookie and sso_cookie name the session cookie and the sign-in's: cookies are per host, not per port, so applications on one host name theirs apart. 6. The refusals The checks raise KeyRefused (callers) and AdminRefused (the admin login), from graph_security.errors , each with an HTTP status , a message, and for 429 a retry_after . Answer them with their status, and on a 401 with a WWW-Authenticate naming the realm for their scope ( Bearer realm="app" , "app-admin" ). Both applications log every refusal in their audit log. Settings The modules read the settings by name ( settings.api_keys , settings.oidc_issuer , ...), from the application's own Settings or a SecuritySettings : give the application's the same fields ( Settings ).

docs.text: TLS between servers For: whoever runs an application's servers on more than one host, or on a network they don't fully trust. You'll find: what is protected and how, the settings, the startup checks, and the functions an application calls. Without it, an application's servers talk over plain HTTP and rely on the network being private. With it, every hop between them is https, each certificate is checked against your own private CA, and a server can answer only callers that present a certificate from it (mutual TLS). It is on in production ( ENVIRONMENT=production ) and off in development: a production server without its certificates refuses to start, naming what is missing. INTERNAL_TLS_REQUIRED=False turns it off in production, with a warning at every start. One call caller server │ ── 1. TLS hello: the server's name ────────────────▶ │ │ ◀─ 2. its certificate (from your CA) ─────────────── │ │ checked against INTERNAL_TLS_CA_FILE, and its name │ │ against the URL (or INTERNAL_TLS_SERVER_NAME) │ │ ◀─ 3. "show me yours" ──────────────────────────────── │ UVICORN_SSL_CERT_REQS=required │ ── 4. its own certificate (INTERNAL_TLS_CERTFILE) ───▶ │ checked against UVICORN_SSL_CA_CERTS │ ══ encrypted from here on ══════════════════════════════│ │ ── 5. the call, with the application's own secret ───▶ │ (PARTITION_TOKEN, REPLICATION_API_KEY) Certificates are always checked. There is no setting to skip the check. Settings A server listening: Setting Default What it does UVICORN_SSL_CERTFILE , UVICORN_SSL_KEYFILE none This server's certificate and key: it speaks https only UVICORN_SSL_CA_CERTS none The CA that callers' client certificates must come from UVICORN_SSL_CERT_REQS none Client certificates: none , optional (checked when given), or required (mutual TLS) A server calling another: Setting Default What it does INTERNAL_TLS_CA_FILE none The CA the other servers' certificates must come from. None: the system's trusted CAs INTERNAL_TLS_CERTFILE , INTERNAL_TLS_KEYFILE none This server's client certificate, sent on every internal call INTERNAL_TLS_SERVER_NAME none Check the application's servers' certificates against this name instead of their URLs' host: for servers with made-up names INTERNAL_TLS_REQUIRED True in production, False in development Internal URLs must be https:// , and this server must speak https; it refuses to start otherwise The startup checks internal_tls.problems(settings, urls) lists what stops a server starting, and the application refuses to start on any: INTERNAL_TLS_REQUIRED=True and this server doesn't speak https, or one of its internal URLs (the urls the application names, such as PARTITION_URLS ) is http:// ; a certificate, key or CA file that isn't there or can't be read; only one of a certificate and its key; UVICORN_SSL_CERT_REQS other than none , optional and required , or required without UVICORN_SSL_CA_CERTS . internal_tls.upgrade_members() turns the http:// server URLs an application kept from before into https:// , with the same host and port, and logs which. In an application Function What internal_tls.uvicorn_options(settings) The keyword arguments for uvicorn.run() : the certificate, key, CA and client-certificate rule internal_tls.opener(settings) A urllib opener for the internal calls: the CA, the client certificate, the server name internal_tls.httpx_client(settings) The same as an httpx.Client (needs httpx ) internal_tls.client_context(settings) The ssl.SSLContext behind both internal_tls.metrics_server_options(settings) The options for a separate metrics port that speaks https the same way internal_tls.problems(settings, {name: [urls]}) The startup checks above The certificates One per server in production, holding the names the others reach it by. A certificate serves and calls (it holds both serverAuth and clientAuth). Keep the CA's key off the servers. Every server needs the CA's certificate, its own certificate and its key, readable by the server's user. Each application has a script that makes a CA and certificates, and its deployment puts them in place: sitelabs-graph-database , sitelabs-partitioned-graph . What it doesn't cover Clients over the internet: put a reverse proxy with a public certificate in front. Services that can't ask for client certificates (Perses): keep their ports private.

docs.text: API keys For: whoever gives clients their keys. You'll find: what a key is, the entry the server holds, changing keys without a restart, a key's last day, and what happens with no keys at all. A client sends its key on every call, as X-API-Key: <key> . Each key has a name (the one in the logs), a role ( Roles and permissions ) and, if you like, a last day . The entry The server never holds a key. It holds an entry for each, comma-separated in API_KEYS : name:role:hash[:YYYY-MM-DD] ann:read:3f1c9e... # ann, who may read loader:write:9a0b47...:2027-03-31 # a key that stops working after 31 March 2027 alex:admin:77d2e1... The hash is the hex SHA-256 of the hex SHA-256 of the key. The server looks a key up by it, so a key can't be guessed by timing. A stolen entry can't be used as a key, nor to log in as an admin: the login needs the key's first hash, which the entry doesn't give away ( Admin login ). A malformed entry stops the server at startup, naming it: an unknown role, a bad hash, a date that isn't one. Give each client its own key, so one can be taken back alone. Each application has a tool that makes a key and prints it once, with its entry (sitelabs-graph-database: scripts/api-key.py ; sitelabs-partitioned-graph: python -m app.tools apikey ). From code, graph_security.keys.new_key(name, role, days=0) returns the key and its entry ( days : how long it lasts; 0, no last day). Changing keys without a restart API_KEYS is read at startup. API_KEYS_FILE names a file of more entries, one a line ( # starts a comment), read again whenever the file changes: a key is added, removed or replaced with no restart. A key removed or replaced stops working at once: its browser sessions and admin logins with it. Setting Default What it does API_KEYS none The entries, comma-separated API_KEYS_FILE none A file of more entries, one a line, read again when it changes A key in both is refused at startup (the same name twice). A key's last day An entry may end with its last day, :YYYY-MM-DD . The key works until the end of that day (UTC), then answers 401 ( the key 'loader' expired at the end of 2027-03-31 ). The server warns at startup from two weeks before. With no keys With no keys at all and no identity provider, every endpoint is open, the admin ones too, with no login. That is for development only: in production ( ENVIRONMENT=production ), a server with no key and no identity provider refuses to start, and so does one whose API_KEYS_FILE holds none. Refusals Answer When 401 No key, a key that isn't in API_KEYS or API_KEYS_FILE , or one past its last day 403 A key whose role hasn't the permission the call needs ( Roles and permissions ) Keys are never logged: only their names.

docs.text: OAuth and OIDC For: whoever wants users and services to log in through an identity provider instead of API keys. You'll find: what it does, the steps to turn it on, each provider's settings, the settings, and what it doesn't do. With OAUTH_OIDC_ACTIVE=True , a server accepts access tokens from an OpenID Connect provider: Keycloak, Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Auth0, Amazon Cognito or any other that issues signed JWTs. The provider holds the users, their passwords and MFA; the server only checks the tokens it is sent, and gives none itself. It is off by default. API keys With OIDC Who the caller is A key's name The token's preferred_username (or the service's client_id ) Their role The key's role A claim in the token, mapped by OIDC_ROLE_MAP A user joins or leaves Edit the keys At the provider; nothing on the server Second factor None Whatever the provider requires Admin endpoints The challenge login with an admin key A token with the admin role, and a recent login if you ask for one An application's own credentials between its servers (sitelabs-partitioned-graph's PARTITION_TOKEN , sitelabs-graph-database's REPLICATION_API_KEY ) don't go to the provider, so it being away never stops them. 1. Put TLS in front A token sent over plain HTTP can be taken and used by anyone who sees it until it expires. Put a reverse proxy with TLS in front of the server before handing out tokens. 2. Set up the provider The API , with an audience, say graph-api . Its tokens must carry it ( aud ). Roles or groups for read, write and admin (and any roles of your own), say graph-read , graph-write , graph-admin . Give them to users and services, and make sure they appear in the access token. A client for each service, with the client credentials grant, given the role it needs. For people, the client they log in with: the device code flow, the provider's CLI, or a web page's client ( Browser sessions ). MFA for everyone with the admin role, and access tokens that last 5 to 15 minutes : a token can't be taken back once issued, only left to expire. Provider OIDC_ISSUER OIDC_ROLE_CLAIM OIDC_AUDIENCE_CLAIM Keycloak https://<host>/realms/<realm> realm_access.roles ; add an audience mapper so aud holds your API aud Microsoft Entra ID https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant id>/v2.0 roles (the app roles you define) aud (the API's application id) Okta https://<org>.okta.com/oauth2/<authorization server> groups (add a groups claim), or scp aud Auth0 https://<tenant>.auth0.com/ , with its final / permissions (with RBAC on), or a namespaced claim an Action adds aud Amazon Cognito https://cognito-idp.<region>.amazonaws.com/<user pool id> cognito:groups client_id : its access tokens have no aud , so OIDC_AUDIENCE is the app client's id 3. Set the server's settings OAUTH_OIDC_ACTIVE=True OIDC_ISSUER=https://idp.example.com/realms/graph OIDC_AUDIENCE=graph-api OIDC_ROLE_CLAIM=realm_access.roles OIDC_ROLE_MAP=admin=graph-admin,write=graph-write,read=graph-read # optional OIDC_ADMIN_MAX_AGE_SECONDS=900 # admin endpoints: a login in the last 15 minutes OIDC_ACCEPT_API_KEYS=True # keys go on working while clients move over The server refuses to start, naming each problem, without one of the four required settings, or with one it can't use: an http:// issuer or JWKS URL elsewhere than this machine; an algorithm that isn't asymmetric ( HS256 ): only RS256 , RS384 , RS512 , ES256 , ES384 , ES512 , PS256 , PS384 , PS512 and EdDSA ; a role map entry naming a role that isn't built in or one of CUSTOM_ROLES . OIDC_* settings set while OAUTH_OIDC_ACTIVE=False have no effect, and the server says so. How a token is checked The signature, with the provider's keys (JWKS), from its discovery document or OIDC_JWKS_URL . They are fetched when the first token arrives, again every OIDC_JWKS_REFRESH_SECONDS (an hour), and when a token names a key the server doesn't have. A server starts even when the provider can't be reached: tokens are refused with 503 until the keys are fetched, and keys already fetched go on being used while it is away. The issuer, the audience (in OIDC_AUDIENCE_CLAIM ), the expiry and nbf , with OIDC_LEEWAY_SECONDS (60) for the clocks. The roles: the claim OIDC_ROLE_CLAIM (a dotted path such as realm_access.roles ), mapped by OIDC_ROLE_MAP , role=value each. A token with none of the mapped values is refused (403). One with several has the permissions of all of them. The caller's name in the logs: OIDC_NAME_CLAIM ( preferred_username ), else client_id , azp or sub . The admin endpoints take a token with the admin role, no challenge login, and with OIDC_ADMIN_MAX_AGE_SECONDS , only if the user logged in that recently ( auth_time ). A refusal says why, without the token: expired, another issuer, not for this API, a key the provider doesn't list, or none of the roles. Tokens are never logged. Turning API keys off Once every client uses tokens, set OIDC_ACCEPT_API_KEYS=False : X-API-Key is refused (401), the admin challenge login is off (403), and the keys are ignored. Leave it True to keep a key as a way in while the provider is down. Settings Setting Default What it does OAUTH_OIDC_ACTIVE False Accept access tokens from an identity provider OIDC_ISSUER none The provider's issuer ( https:// ): its discovery document is read from there OIDC_AUDIENCE none The audience a token must be for OIDC_ROLE_CLAIM none The claim that holds the roles OIDC_ROLE_MAP none role=value each: which claim value gives which role OIDC_AUDIENCE_CLAIM aud Where the audience is ( client_id for Cognito) OIDC_NAME_CLAIM preferred_username The caller's name in the logs OIDC_JWKS_URL the discovery document's The provider's keys OIDC_ALGORITHMS RS256,ES256 Signatures accepted: asymmetric ones only OIDC_LEEWAY_SECONDS 60 Allowed for the clocks OIDC_JWKS_REFRESH_SECONDS 3600 How often the keys are fetched again OIDC_ADMIN_MAX_AGE_SECONDS 0 (any) The admin endpoints need a login this recent OIDC_ACCEPT_API_KEYS True API keys and the admin login still work too The settings for a web page's sign-in ( OIDC_CONSOLE_* ) are in Browser sessions . What it doesn't do Take a token back before it expires: not possible with a JWT. Keep access tokens short. Issue tokens. The server only checks them.

docs.text: Rate limits For: whoever runs a server that several clients share. You'll find: the limit on calls a second and the limit on work at once, per caller and per role, and what a client sees past them. docs.text: Roles and permissions For: whoever gives clients their keys or their roles at the identity provider, and developers of an application. You'll find: how permissions and roles work, the built-in roles, making roles of your own, how keys, tokens and sessions get a role, and what a refusal says. Every call needs a permission . A caller has a role , and a role is a set of permissions. Permissions are the application's Each application names its permissions in a catalogue , and says which each endpoint needs. Some are admin permissions : they need an admin login , or a token from the identity provider, as well as the role. Its permissions sitelabs-graph-database query , write , load ; admin: manage , backup , repair , leadership , diagnostics , procedures ( its page ) sitelabs-partitioned-graph query , export , algorithms , write , delete , load ; admin: standbys , resize , rollback , suspend , raise_deletes ( its page ) from graph_security.roles import Catalogue, use CATALOGUE = use(Catalogue( {"query": "read queries", "write": "write queries", "load": "bulk loads", "manage": "the platform"}, read={"query"}, write={"write", "load"}, admin_only={"manage"})) The built-in roles Role Permissions read The catalogue's read set write read's, and the write set admin Every permission: write's with its key, and the admin permissions after logging in Roles of your own CUSTOM_ROLES holds them, comma-separated, each name=base , then -permission to take one away or +permission to add one: CUSTOM_ROLES=feeder=read+load,writer=write-load,operator=admin-manage A name is lower case: letters, digits, _ and - , starting with a letter, up to 32 characters, and not read , write or admin . Only a role built on admin may log in as an admin, and admin permissions can be added to no other role: x=write+manage is refused. A role with nothing left, or an unknown permission, is refused. The server names the entry and refuses to start. Roles are read at startup. Changing CUSTOM_ROLES takes a restart; keys can change without one ( API keys ). How a caller gets a role An API key names its role in its entry, name:role:hash , which may be a role of your own ( API keys ). A token from the identity provider gets its roles from OIDC_ROLE_MAP , which may map a group to a role of your own: OIDC_ROLE_MAP=feeder=graph-feeders . A token with several roles has the permissions of all of them ( OAuth and OIDC ). A browser session keeps only query , whatever its role ( Browser sessions ). So an application whose read permission isn't called query gets sessions that do nothing. With no keys and no identity provider (development), every caller has every permission. Refusals A call without the permission answers 403 , naming the permission, what it covers, the caller and their role: {"error": "this needs the load permission (bulk loads); 'ann' has the role feeder, which hasn't it"} The application decides what else a refusal does: both audit every refusal. What roles don't do No rules per label or property. A role that may query reads the whole graph. Put finer rules in the application in front of the server.

docs.text: Browser sessions For: whoever sets up a web page (a query console, dashboards) for people, not programs. You'll find: signing in at the identity provider or with a key, what a session may do, the cookie, the endpoints, and the settings. A browser can stay signed in to a server, so a page needs no key typed each time. The session is a cookie the server sets; the browser never holds a key or a token. Signing in At the identity provider (with OIDC_CONSOLE_CLIENT_ID ): the page sends the browser to /console/sso/start , which sends it on to the provider's sign-in page. It comes back to /console/sso/callback with a code, which the server exchanges for an access token itself (the authorization code flow, with PKCE). It checks the token as it checks every token ( OAuth and OIDC ), then sets the cookie. The token never reaches the browser. With a key: the page sends it once, POST /session with X-API-Key , and forgets it. From a script: POST /session with X-API-Key or Authorization: Bearer sets the same cookie. Signing out ( DELETE /session ) drops the cookie, and the server remembers that session ended. GET /session says who is signed in, and until when. What a session may do Only read. Of its role's permissions a session keeps query alone: it can't write, load or log in as an admin, whatever its role. A leaked cookie can't change the graph. A session made with a key ends with the key: removed from API_KEYS_FILE , replaced or expired, it stops working at the next call. A session from the identity provider keeps the role it signed in with until it ends, after SESSION_SECONDS (8 hours). Taking someone's role away at the provider counts from their next sign-in. A role without query can't make a session (403): it would do nothing. The cookie HttpOnly (no script can read it), SameSite=Strict (no other site's page can send it) and, over https, Secure . Signed with SESSION_SECRET (HMAC-SHA256). Give every server of an application the same one, and a session works at all of them, and across a restart. Without it, a secret is made at startup, and a restart signs everyone out. Named by the application: cookies are per host, not per port, so two applications on one host name theirs apart (sitelabs-graph-database: graphdb_session ; sitelabs-partitioned-graph: pgraph_session ). Settings Setting Default What it does SESSION_SECRET made at startup Signs the sessions and the admin logins: 32 characters or more, the same on every server SESSION_SECONDS 28800 How long a session lasts after signing in OIDC_CONSOLE_CLIENT_ID none The page's client at the identity provider: signing in there needs it OIDC_CONSOLE_SCOPES openid profile The scopes it asks for. Add the API's own when the provider needs one for the token's audience (Entra ID: api://<id>/.default ; Cognito: its resource server's scope) OIDC_CONSOLE_AUTH_PARAMS none More parameters for the provider's sign-in page: audience=graph-api for Auth0 OIDC_CONSOLE_REDIRECT_URI <this server>/console/sso/callback Where the provider sends the browser back, when the address the server sees isn't the one the browser uses At the identity provider A public client (no secret) using the authorization code flow with PKCE . Its id is OIDC_CONSOLE_CLIENT_ID . Its redirect URI is https://<the server's public name>/console/sso/callback , exactly. Its access tokens must be the API's like any client's: the audience OIDC_AUDIENCE , and the roles in OIDC_ROLE_CLAIM . The server calls the provider's token endpoint itself, so it must reach it. Behind a reverse proxy, the callback address comes from the request: the proxy must pass the Host header, and the server must believe its X-Forwarded-Proto ( UVICORN_FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS ). Else set OIDC_CONSOLE_REDIRECT_URI . Behind a load balancer with several servers, set it to the public address, so the callback names it whichever server answers. Every sign-in, refused or not, and every sign-out goes to the application's audit hook ( session.start , session.end ).
